transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Rohan Gupta (Redwood Infra), Diana Park (CTO, Bluehaven), Evan Ruiz (ML Platform), Priya Shah (Security), Marco Li (SRE)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive focused on delivering Redwood for an airwalled on-prem site. Topics: sealed package / sideload delivery, offline licensing / notarization, signed GPU driver bundles, runtime perf when running quantized weights, KV cache behaviors for high-prefix reuse workloads, batching configs for sub-20ms token latency targets, and required firewall/VPC rules for the transfer protocol.

Topics (auto): offline artifact delivery, signed drivers, quantization impact on throughput, kv cache warm-up, batching tradeoffs, offline licensing flow, network allowlist.

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll do a quick intros round and then Samir will drive the technical flow. I know Bluehaven is airwalled so we'll focus on sealed packages and the offline licensing dance.
[00:00:18] Diana Park: thanks, Ava. For context, we're an internal inference platform for clinical note summarization, so latency is a big deal but data never leaves the facility. we want deterministic behavior, and we have a small fleet of A100 and an older batch of 2080Ti nodes.
[00:00:35] Evan Ruiz: yeah, and we have a KV-store in front but the cache hit rate is variable — sometimes it's 40% on some cohorts. hoping for best practices on prefix caching and cold-starts.
[00:00:47] Samir Patel: Great. The plan: walk through the sealed-package format, the delivery handshake, driver signing, and then runtime tuning — batching, quantization tradeoffs, KV cache warm-up heuristics. We'll sprinkle in specific firewall rules.
[00:01:02] Priya Shah: quick ask — we need the exact offline licensing protocol mapped to our internal PKI. We can't do any external callback to a public license server. So we need a notarized token exchange that we can validate locally.
[00:01:18] Rohan Gupta: and from infra side, if packages are >20GB we need chunking with resume support and checksums.
[00:01:27] Samir Patel: Absolutely. Redwood's sealed-package flow supports chunked transfer with sha256 per chunk and an overall manifest. For airgapped installs we provide a signed manifest and a notarized license blob that you can validate against our public signing cert — we also support pre-loading the cert into your HSM.
[00:01:45] Marco Li: HSM integration is key. Our cluster uses HSM-backed key store for signing images internally. Does Redwood support importing the Redwood signing cert into our HSM?
[00:01:58] Ava Martinez: Yes, we can provide a cert bundle. In the private deployment guide we have steps for pinning the Redwood CA cert into customer KMS/HSM and validating the signature locally. We'll attach the doc.
[00:02:12] [00:02:12] Samir Patel: Now on driver bundles — two asks: one, we produce signed GPU driver + kernel modules only when customers request; two, we publish a compatibility matrix. for your A100s we generally recommend NVIDIA 525.x, but the older 2080Ti are on 470.x series which we can support but require different compiled kernels.
[00:02:36] Evan Ruiz: so we'll need two different driver artifacts? that increases artifact count and transfer complexity.
[00:02:42] Samir Patel: Yes. We can produce per-SKU signed bundles. Each bundle is individually signed and checksummed. Transfer manifest lists bundles and we'll only install ones that match hardware. That keeps the runtime lean.
[00:02:55] Diana Park: any concerns with driver licensing from Nvidia? we have to ensure vendor EULA is respected when we sideload drivers airgapped.
[00:03:04] Rohan Gupta: they may require the driver binary to be kept under a vendor-specified distro. we need compliance vetting.
[00:03:10] Samir Patel: good point. We typically provide the recommendation to rekey or re-package the driver under the customer's internal distro, and we will provide the build scripts. We'll also include a small verification shim so that the Redwood runtime can detect expected driver module versions.
[00:03:25] [00:03:25] Samir Patel: moving into runtime perf: quantization can reduce memory footprint and increase throughput, but there's a quality vs latency trade. for a chat/summarization workload with short prompts you can often go 8-bit or 4-bit quant and get 1.6–2.5x throughput gains depending on kernel support. if you need strict deterministic outputs, we recommend running eval prompts against quantized weights first.
[00:03:49] Evan Ruiz: we're sensitive to hallucinations in clinical text. if quantization changes outputs slightly that's a risk. can we run a canary with a few hundred prompts?
[00:03:58] Samir Patel: yes, that's standard. Redwood Optimize can produce a regression report comparing baseline fp16 to int8/int4 quant under your prompt sets. we'll do a per-prompt delta and estimate token-level divergence.
[00:04:12] Priya Shah: is there any offline tooling to perform quantization without internet access? we need to do this inside the airgapped lab.
[00:04:20] Samir Patel: we provide a CLI tool inside the sealed package that performs offline quantization and outputs a sha256-signed artifact. It relies on local compute only; no external calls. We'll include the quantize binary in the artifact.
[00:04:35] [00:04:35] Rohan Gupta: about KV cache — our workload has heavy prefix reuse: many notes begin with the same header and past context. what's Redwood's recommendation to warm the cache in an airgapped environment?
[00:04:47] Samir Patel: Two approaches: pre-warm via a one-time replay using a deduped list of prefixes shipped inside the package; or baseline warmers that run at boot and replay high-frequency prefixes. We also expose metrics to track KV-hit-rate and can advise a dynamic eviction TTL. note that early requests may see cold-cache latency, so plan for a ramp.
[00:05:08] Marco Li: how big is the kv cache memory footprint per model? we have 80GB of GPU RAM on some nodes but also small nodes.
[00:05:18] Samir Patel: depends on sequence length and model. For 2k context on a 7B model kv cache per token is modest but for 20k context it grows linearly. We'll provide model-specific profiles. For your configs we estimated about 12GB per GPU reserved for KV for long-context runs if you keep a 16k window.
[00:05:36] [00:05:36] Evan Ruiz: batching — we want sub-20ms token latency for a subset of requests and higher throughput for background summarization jobs. can Redwood do policy routing between low-latency nodes and high-throughput nodes?
[00:05:50] Samir Patel: Yes. You can create route policies in the config that pin to a "low-latency pool" (min batch size = 1, small GPU count, strict preemption) and a "throughput pool" (larger batch sizes, lower GPU per host). The runtime supports continuous batching and will respect SLO hints.
[00:06:08] Diana Park: preemption — how do we ensure low-latency jobs preempt big-batch jobs without causing instability?
[00:06:15] Rohan Gupta: also, what's the cost of preemption in terms of wasted tokens?
[00:06:20] Samir Patel: Preemption is cooperative. Large-batch runners checkpoint prefix state and the runtime can snapshot the KV cache to disk to allow quick resumption, but there is some overhead. In practice we've seen <2% wasted tokens if policies are tuned. We'll share observed metrics from a similar customer.
[00:06:35] [00:06:35] Priya Shah: network/firewall specifics: what ports and DNS access are required for the sealed-package transfer and offline licensing handshake? we can't allow outbound to public internet in production.
[00:06:48] Samir Patel: For airgapped, transfer is typically via scp of the sealed-package delivered on an external vault drive, or via an internal transfer server you stand up that we validate with signed manifests. The offline licensing handshake is an exchange of signed blobs — you can validate signatures locally. Only exception is if you opt in to remote attestation; that requires outbound to our attestation endpoint.
[00:07:08] Marco Li: are there checksums per chunk? what happens if transfer interrupted mid-chunk?
[00:07:13] Samir Patel: The chunking protocol supports resume at chunk boundaries and per-chunk sha256. The installer will refuse a corrupted chunk. We also include an installer verification phase that ensures all components have expected signatures.
[00:07:25] [00:07:25] Evan Ruiz: about observability — will Redwood Console run inside airgapped? we need logs and traces forwarded to our internal ELK stack.
[00:07:34] Rohan Gupta: and we need token-level cost breakdowns — can that be computed offline?
[00:07:39] Ava Martinez: We ship an on-prem observability agent that writes telemetry to your internal endpoints. For cost breakdown we can provide offline aggregators that compute token counts and cost model locally; the Console has an offline mode for private deployments.
[00:07:53] [00:07:53] Diana Park: security review: Priya — anything else from your side?
[00:07:56] Priya Shah: we'll need SOC2 artifacts and a list of Redwood's internal access controls. also a copy of the code-signing cert and the public key fingerprint. our security policy requires key rotation guidance.
[00:08:09] Samir Patel: We'll provide SOC2 plus a signing-cert rotation guide. For key rotation we recommend a quarterly cadence and we provide tooling to re-sign manifests in-house if you need to rekey.
[00:08:22] [00:08:22] Rohan Gupta: one more infra twist: can we run Redwood runtime inside our VPC behind a private NAT, or does it require host-level kernel modules?
[00:08:33] Samir Patel: The runtime runs as a containerized service and requires specific kernel modules only for the GPU drivers. We don't require any special host kernel mods beyond standard NVIDIA module compatibility. Network-wise, it can live fully inside your VPC with no egress. For admin flows you can use our private control plane in airgapped mode which talks over pre-shared signed messages.
[00:08:53] Marco Li: if we go with full airgap, how do we get security patches to the runtime?
[00:08:58] Samir Patel: We publish patch bundles that you can pull via offline transfer; the bundles are signed and include delta patches to reduce transfer size. For critical security fixes we can ship a small patch bundle that's usually <50MB.
[00:09:10] [00:09:10] Evan Ruiz: curious about performance numbers — can you share a rough benchmark for 7B quantized vs fp16 for throughput and p50 latency?
[00:09:19] Samir Patel: Rough numbers on an A100 with optimized kernels: fp16 p50 token latency ~8ms, throughput ~350 tokens/s per GPU depending on batch shape. int8/int4 quant could push throughput to 600–800 tokens/s but p50 may slightly increase if we need extra dequant steps; depends on kernel. We'll provide a benchmark sheet.
[00:09:36] Diana Park: can you run a benchmark using our workload? transferring a small sample dataset for offline benchmarking is fine.
[00:09:43] Samir Patel: Yes, we can run an offline benchmark. We'll need a small prompt corpus and model variant choice. We can deliver the benchmark runner in the sealed-package and you can run it in your secure lab; results can be shared as a signed report.
[00:09:55] [00:09:55] Priya Shah: legal: offline licensing — will we be forced to call home for license renewal? we need multi-year offline renewals.
[00:10:04] Ava Martinez: We support multi-year offline license blobs that are notarized and can be validated locally. Renewal can happen via a signed renewal blob exchange and does not require outbound connectivity if you prefer manual renewals.
[00:10:15] [00:10:15] Rohan Gupta: ok let's talk concretely about the dry-run: what do you need from us next week?
[00:10:21] Samir Patel: To run a dry-run we need: (1) GPU inventory + OS/kernel versions, (2) sample prompt set for benchmarking, (3) a staging node with analogous network restrictions for the installer to run, (4) contact for HSM integration. We'll create a checklist.
[00:10:35] Diana Park: we can provide (1) and (2) by Friday. staging node might take a week. HSM person is Priya.
[00:10:42] Priya Shah: yep I'll coordinate.
[00:10:45] [00:10:45] Samir Patel: Great. Closing sections: Risks/mitigations — driver EULA, quantization output drift, initial KV cold start latency, transfer corruption. Mitigations: signed bundles + manifest, local eval canaries, pre-warmers for KV, chunked transfers with resume and per-chunk SHA.
[00:11:12] Marco Li: that sounds good. Any plan B if kernel mismatch prevents driver install?
[00:11:18] Samir Patel: Plan B is to run a remote-exec container that uses user-space GPU runtime (where possible) or fallback to smaller models that fit on CPU for critical lanes while we work the kernel patch. We'll list compatible fallbacks.
[00:11:32] [00:11:32] Ava Martinez: we'll follow up with a manifest, sealed-package checklist, and the benchmark runner. Also Samir will send the signed-driver compatibility matrix.
[00:11:42] Diana Park: thanks. quick note: please mark all docs with internal classification 'For Bluehaven Use Only' before we ingest them into our vault.
[00:11:50] Evan Ruiz: and can we get an estimate of transfer time for a full bundle? ballpark for 80GB over our secure internal link?
[00:11:57] Samir Patel: if your internal transfer speed is ~500MB/s you'd finish in under 3 minutes for 80GB, but typical secure transfers with checksum and throttling take longer — expect 30–60 minutes with verification. We'll provide a transfer estimator.
[00:12:14] [00:12:14] Recap & Next Steps:
- Redwood to share sealed-package transfer checklist, chunking protocol doc, and the driver compatibility matrix (Samir)
- Bluehaven to send GPU list + sample prompts (Diana/Evan)
- Schedule dry-run week of 2025-10-20 (Ava to coordinate timelines)
- Security: Samir & Priya to align on certificate import and rotation plan

End of transcript.
